result:
I've been thinking about rivers, and specifically about the fact that a river isn't a thing. It's an argument.

Here's the mechanism, which I find genuinely beautiful. Water moving around a bend travels faster on the outside of the curve and slower on the inside. Fast water carries sediment; slow water drops it. So the outer bank erodes and the inner bank builds up, which means the bend gets *bendier*, which means the speed difference gets more pronounced, which means the bend gets bendier still. It's a runaway process. Any trivial irregularity in the channel — a fallen log, a slightly harder patch of clay — becomes the seed of a curve that will eventually swing a mile wide.

There's a second layer to it. The water in a bend doesn't just go around, it corkscrews. Helical flow: down at the outer bank, across the bottom, up at the inner bank, back across the surface. So the river is constantly shoveling material from the place it's tearing down to the place it's building up. It's a conveyor belt made of nothing but water obeying physics.

And the whole pattern migrates. Meanders creep downstream like a wave traveling along a rope, so the same bend that undercuts your property this decade will be undercutting your neighbor's in fifty years. Sometimes a loop swings so far that its own neck pinches shut, the river takes the shortcut, and the abandoned curve is left behind as a crescent of still water. An oxbow lake. A sentence the river started and decided not to finish.

In 1996 a geologist named Hans-Henrik Stølum published a paper claiming that if you measure a river's actual winding length and divide by its straight-line distance, the number tends toward pi. This is contested — the data are thin, the averaging is doing a lot of work — but I'm less interested in whether it's true than in how badly people wanted it to be. There's something in us that hopes the mess resolves into a constant. That the wandering is secretly disciplined.

The thing I keep returning to, though, is a set of maps.

In 1944 the Army Corps of Engineers published an atlas by a cartographer named Harold Fisk, showing the historical courses of the Lower Mississippi. Fisk read the floodplain the way you'd read tree rings — old channels leave distinctive deposits, and if you core enough of them you can reconstruct where the river used to be. The resulting maps show every past course at once, in different colors, all overlapping: ribbons of pink and blue and ochre looping and crossing and doubling back across the same terrain. They look like nerve tissue. They look like someone's handwriting practiced over and over on the same page.

What gets me is that the present-day river, drawn in among all that, doesn't look special. It's one ribbon among twenty. It has no more claim to being *the* Mississippi than any of the others; it's just the one that happens to have water in it right now. The river's whole biography is spread out flat, simultaneous, and the current moment is barely distinguishable from the discarded drafts.

There's a temptation here to make this into a tidy metaphor about memory and I want to resist it slightly, because the actual situation is stranger than the metaphor would be. The river doesn't remember anything. Water has no history; each molecule arrives, does its brief work on the bank, and leaves. The remembering is done entirely by the land. The floodplain is the archive and the river is the illiterate author, endlessly revising a document it can't read.

That asymmetry seems important and I can't quite say why. Maybe it's that we tend to imagine memory as something a thing does to hold onto its own past, and here it's the opposite — the past is held by everything the river touched, on the river's behalf, whether or not it wanted a record kept. The evidence is external. It's in the deposits, the grain sizes, the way certain soils drain and certain crops fail in mysterious curved patterns that turn out to trace a channel abandoned nine hundred years ago. Farmers in Louisiana plow across the ghosts of bends.

I suppose the thing I actually like about rivers is that they demonstrate you can get enormous, apparently deliberate structure out of a process with no plan in it whatsoever. The meander isn't designed. Nobody chose pi. It's just what happens when water is heavy and banks are soft and time is long. And the result is a shape that looks so much like intention that we've spent centuries writing poems about the river's *wisdom*, its patience, its knowing where to go.

It doesn't know. It's just falling, and the falling has a texture.

I think that's enough to have earned the ending. The loop pinches off; the water takes the short way; something crescent-shaped is left behind, going still.
